terms.grammar: adverb; the verb in the mood of the condition it stands for
evidence: Cic. Off. 2.42: neque enim aliter esset jūs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: “If not, …”: aliter stands for a condition, so after an unreal one the verb is subjunctive (aliter esset, otherwise it would be). Its first sense is “in another way” (aliter atque, otherwise than).

terms.grammar: conjunction and adverb, opening a clause
evidence: Cic. Att. 1.2.1: sīn aliter acciderit, hūmāniter ferēmus
terms.comment: Where the “otherwise” is a whole condition: see if not.

evidence: Plin. Ep. 8.8.1: sī nōndum (et putō nōndum: aliōquī narrāssēs mihi) (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: From Livy on, and frequent in Pliny’s letters and Quintilian; not in Cicero (Lewis & Short). Lewis & Short notes that the form aliōquīn is doubted in the manuscripts.

phrases.latin: jūs enim semper est quaesītum aequābile; neque enim aliter esset jūs
phrases.english: for what was always sought was fair and equal law; otherwise it would not be law
but if it turns out otherwise, we shall bear it like reasonable people

phrases.latin: sī nōndum (et putō nōndum: aliōquī narrāssēs mihi)
phrases.english: if you haven’t yet (and I think you haven’t, otherwise you would have told me)

sources: Lewis & Short: aliter · Lewis & Short: sin · Lewis & Short: alioqui

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
